e.t: Abama is a proper name rendered as “Abama” or “Avama” in the Greek Septuagint. It functions as a name rather than a common descriptive word. The word occurs twice in the Greek Septuagint, with both occurrences located in Ezekiel 20:29. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name’s particular reference cannot be identified from the word alone.

This word means “helplessness”: the condition of being without effective help or power to deal with a need. It is a noun, so it names a state or condition rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Sirach 51:10. That single occurrence indicates a focused use of the word, while the basic meaning remains the condition of lacking help. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word refers to grass that mules fed on. It is a noun naming a particular kind of grass or fodder, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines how that grass functions in the sentence. The word is therefore a concrete term for vegetation used as food by working animals.

Adi is a proper name, identified with the forms “Adi” and “Athi.” In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 11:27. As a proper name, it functions to identify a particular named individual rather than to describe an action, quality, or general concept. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identification, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain the individual’s role in that passage.

This adjective describes something clear or bright. It can refer to a condition marked by openness, brightness, or the absence of cloudiness, depending on the sentence in which it appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, appearing seven verses in Job and Ezekiel. Its basic idea remains straightforward: what is clear, bright, or unclouded. The surrounding verse determines whether the description concerns appearance, the sky, light, or another visible condition.

Amouk is a proper name, referring to a person named Amouk, also rendered Amuk. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 12:20. The available information identifies the name but does not provide a separate word meaning or description of the person. Its ordinary function is simply to identify that individual in the passage where the name occurs; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain that passage further.

“Anag” is a proper name, used to identify a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than to describe a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 37:13. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough context to identify exactly what or whom Anag names in that verse. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding passage, while its basic function is that of a specific name.

Anathōthia, also written Anathothia, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament, while the available information does not specify whether that name refers to a person, place, or another named subject. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 8:24. Its precise reference there requires the surrounding verse text for further explanation.

This Greek LXX verb means to throw the head back. It describes a physical movement in which someone tilts or raises the head backward. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, and Nehemiah. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains this bodily action rather than a general attitude or decision.

This Greek LXX verb means “kindled” or “lit up,” describing something being set alight or beginning to burn brightly. It expresses the act or result of ignition rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Jeremiah 31:9, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is becoming kindled or lit up.

This Greek LXX verb means “dedicate” or “devote”: it describes the act of setting something or someone apart for a particular purpose. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 3 Maccabees 7:20. The precise object being dedicated and the force of the action depend on the surrounding verse context.

gl: upper crossbeam of the loom; heddle-rod
d: upper crossbeam of the loom; heddle-rod

e.t: This word refers to the “upper crossbeam of the loom” or a “heddle-rod,” a wooden part used in weaving. It is a noun naming a physical tool rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in descriptions involving weapons or implements associated with warfare. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains this structural part of a loom.

This verb means to remove something or take it away. It describes an action in which a person, object, or thing is lifted from its present place or separated from what it was with. The word occurs 116 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is a recurring way to express movement or removal. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what is being removed and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “blow away,” describing the act of sending something away by blowing. It presents removal through a forceful breath or gust rather than simply moving something by hand. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Hosea 13:3. Its precise force in that verse is determined by the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the dispersing or driving away of something by blowing.

This noun means “chief cook” or “dignitary”: it can identify a person responsible for cooking at a high level or a person of high rank. The word is therefore a title or designation for an individual, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 22 times across 22 verses, showing repeated use for an established office or status. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Asiēli, also rendered Asili, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:48. Because a proper name identifies a person, its meaning here is primarily its identifying function; the surrounding verse is needed to say more about the individual associated with it.

This adjective describes a place that has no wall or other fortification around it—something “unwalled” or “unfortified.” It is a physical description of a settlement or location lacking defensive protection, rather than a title or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers 13:19 and Proverbs 32:28. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the absence of enclosing defenses.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Atoupha” or “Atufa.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 2:54. The name itself gives no further meaning beyond identifying the individual, so the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand that person’s specific role or setting. Both “Atoupha” and “Atufa” represent the same name in this LXX occurrence.

Aphek, also rendered Afek, is a proper name for a place rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times, referring to named locations in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 2 Kings. Because it is a place-name, its meaning is primarily its identifying name; the surrounding verse is needed to understand what occurred at any particular Aphek.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Bagoui” or “Vagoi.” It is not a description of a quality, action, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 2:2, within a list of people connected with the return from exile. Its exact significance beyond identifying that person is not given by the word itself.

Bale, also rendered Vale, is a proper name used to identify someone or something specifically named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general description or action word, but as a name. The name occurs seven times in the LXX corpus, including passages in Numbers and 1 Chronicles, and once in Proverbs. Its precise reference may depend on the surrounding verse, but its basic function is as a personal or named designation.

This word is a proper name, given as “Bēbai; Vive,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The form appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 10:16. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name’s precise reference in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic function is to identify a person by name.

This word means “palace,” referring to a grand or official residence associated with a ruler or government. It is a noun, so it names a place rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:2. The word’s central idea is a prominent residence or administrative building, not an ordinary private home. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person or setting being described there.

This Greek LXX noun means “food”—what people or animals eat for nourishment. It can refer broadly to provisions or something prepared to be eaten, rather than to one particular dish. The word occurs 71 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing ordinary use for edible sustenance in varied settings. Its precise force in a particular passage comes from the surrounding sentence and situation.

This proper noun refers to a place named “Gaulōn,” also rendered “Gavlon.” It is a place-name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Joshua. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and its context, but the name itself identifies Gaulōn. The form is preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive English word.

This word means “geometry,” referring to the study or practice of measuring and describing space, shapes, and their dimensions. It is a noun, so it names a subject or activity rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 34:11. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the mathematical understanding of size, form, and measurement.

This LXX Greek verb means “darken”: to make something dark or to become dark. As a verb, it describes a change in brightness or visibility rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Lamentations 2:1. The word’s exact force there must be understood from the verse and its surrounding passage, but its basic idea remains the loss or covering of light.

This noun means “plunder”: goods or possessions seized from others, especially in the aftermath of conquest, attack, or judgment. It describes what is taken rather than the act of taking it. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical text, it occurs 13 times, showing a recurring term for property carried away or claimed through violence. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “diffusion,” describing the spreading or dispersal of something from one area into another. It names a process rather than a person or action commanded by itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek text of Leviticus, in Leviticus 13:27, 13:35, and 14:48. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being described there, but its central sense remains the movement or spread of something outward.

This Greek LXX verb means “thirsty”: it describes experiencing a need or desire for water. It functions as an action or condition word, telling what someone is feeling rather than naming the water itself. The word occurs 35 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, so it can describe ordinary physical thirst wherever the context presents that condition. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “present”—something given to another person, often as an offering. Its central idea is a bestowed item rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 93 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used broadly, including in passages connected with offerings. Its precise significance in any verse depends on what is being presented and to whom, but the basic meaning remains a present given or offered.

This adjective means “circular” or “rounded,” describing something shaped like a circle or having a curved, enclosing form. It is a Greek LXX word preserved in the Old Testament Greek text and occurs once, in Daniel 4:37. The word itself gives a basic description of shape; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage. It should therefore be understood as a physical or descriptive term rather than expanded into an unrelated figurative meaning.

This verb means “implement”: to put something into effect or carry it out. It describes the action of fulfilling or executing what has been intended, commanded, or arranged. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being implemented in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “evacuate”: to leave a place or cause people to leave it. It describes a deliberate departure or clearing out, rather than simply remaining absent. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Numbers, Judges, Amos, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is leaving and what place is being vacated.

This Greek LXX adverb means “in” or “within,” pointing to a location or position inside something. It describes where someone or something is, rather than naming the object itself. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea remains consistent: being inside a place, object, boundary, or situation. The surrounding words determine exactly what it is within, but the word itself expresses inward location or position.

This Greek LXX noun means “activity”: something being carried out, exerted, or put into operation. It names active working rather than merely a possibility or intention. In its deuterocanonical LXX usage, it occurs eight times across Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. The word appears in passages such as Wisdom 7:17 and 2 Maccabees 3:29, but the surrounding verse is needed to identify exactly whose activity is meant or what it accomplishes.

This verb means to “bury; embalm,” describing the care given to a dead body for burial. It refers to an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within Genesis 50:2, so its recorded use is concentrated in one burial-related setting. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic sense is preparing or placing the dead for burial.

This Greek LXX verb means “dislocate”: to force a joint out of its normal position. It describes a physical action rather than a general feeling or attitude. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 10:5. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its immediate setting, while its basic meaning remains the act of dislocating.

This noun refers to a person or thing treated as an object of contempt—something regarded with scorn, rejection, or very low esteem. It expresses how someone or something is viewed, rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Psalm 21:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains a despised or scorned object.

This verb means “strike upon,” describing an action directed onto something. It presents striking as an act that reaches or lands upon its object, rather than merely existing or moving generally. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:26. The reference identifies where the word appears, but the precise force of the action in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “yearn”: to long for someone or something with strong desire. It describes an inward longing rather than a simple passing preference. The word appears nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including several Psalms, where longing is directed toward God or toward what is deeply desired. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “spitting on,” referring to the act of spitting upon someone or something. It names an action rather than a person, quality, or teaching. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Isaiah 50:6. That reference identifies its location, but the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This verb means to fix something firmly or to support it. It describes establishing something so that it remains secure rather than loose or unstable. In its Greek Old Testament use, it occurs once, in Proverbs 30:28, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains clear: something is held in place, strengthened, or made secure. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation corpus.

This noun means “dress” or “outfit”—clothing considered as what a person wears. It refers to a person’s attire rather than to an action or inner quality. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding wording determines the precise significance of the clothing in each passage, but the word itself has the straightforward sense of apparel or dress. [p03:word:lxx:L705493:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705493:occurrences]

This adjective describes someone or something regarded as contemptible—easy to be despised. It expresses low regard or a condition that invites scorn, rather than honor or respect. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Jeremiah and once in Daniel, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in either passage depends on what person or thing the sentence describes.

Eupatōr, also rendered Efpator, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Maccabees 6:17. Because the available record does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name itself identifies the person but does not by itself explain that person’s role or significance in the passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Zaira” or “Zera.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:16. The name’s precise significance cannot be determined from the name alone, and the available information does not provide surrounding verse text or additional lexical explanation. Its role is therefore best understood simply as the personal name Zaira or Zera in that genealogy.

The word is a proper name: “Thamnasarach” or “Thamnasarakh.” It does not describe an action or quality; it identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament wording. It occurs three times in the LXX, in two verses in Joshua, so its meaning is primarily identifying rather than describing. The exact referent and significance must be understood from the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

This noun means “foundation,” the supporting base on which something is built or established. It can refer to a physical foundation, such as the base of a building, and can also describe the underlying support of something viewed as firmly established. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains the same: a foundational support or base, whether the immediate setting concerns a structure or something pictured as being firmly grounded.

Ieddoua, also rendered Ieththua, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 10:22. The name identifies a particular person in that passage, but the available information does not establish the person’s role or provide a broader meaning for the name itself. Its precise significance in Nehemiah 10:22 must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun means “cheerfulness,” describing a glad, willing disposition rather than sorrow or reluctance. It names an inward quality or attitude that can be expressed in a person’s conduct. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, the word occurs once, in Proverbs 18:22. The reference identifies its occurrence, but the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage. Its central idea remains a cheerful spirit or manner.

“Sharing equally” describes something distributed on an equal basis, with each person receiving an equal share. As an adjective, the word characterizes a person, group, or arrangement marked by equal participation or allotment. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 8:30. The central idea is fairness in the distribution of what is shared; the word emphasizes equal portions rather than merely taking part together.

Iōykam, also called Iukam, is a personal name identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. As a proper name, its meaning is tied to the person it names; no separate descriptive definition is provided. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, at Genesis 36:27. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person named there.

This LXX verb means “see clearly”—to perceive something plainly or distinctly. It describes an act of direct, understandable sight rather than a vague impression. As a verb, it tells what someone sees or perceives. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this LXX corpus, including passages from Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Job, Baruch, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being seen and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “covering; concealment”—something that hides, shields, or keeps something from view. It describes the idea of covering rather than an action, person, or object by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 41:26. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. This word’s central idea remains concealment: placing a covering over something or keeping it hidden from sight.

Cassia is the name of an aromatic spice or fragrant plant product. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun appears once, in Job 42:14. Its basic meaning identifies the substance itself rather than an action, quality, or person. The single occurrence indicates a specialized word used for a particular fragrant material, while the surrounding verse determines its precise role there. This is the LXX Greek word and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament corpus.

This Greek LXX verb means “pull down,” describing the act of bringing something from a higher place to a lower one. It can refer to physically lowering or removing something, and its normal use may also describe bringing someone or something down from an elevated position. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with several occurrences in Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “lord it over” or “master,” describing the exercise of authority or control over others. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for ruling or gaining mastery, whether in humanity’s appointed dominion, control over an enemy, or the authority one person holds over another. It occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, from Genesis through 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This adjective means “set with stones.” It describes an object whose surface or arrangement includes stones placed in it, rather than naming the stones themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, both times in Exodus, so its use is narrow and concrete. The word points to a stone-set or stone-adorned object, while the surrounding passage determines exactly what object is being described.

This noun means “planting” or “plantation”—something planted or an area established with plants. It refers to the result or place of putting plants into the ground, rather than to the act described in detail. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 38:22, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains a planted growth or cultivated planting.

Keroe is a proper name, referring to a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Joshua 19:38, and is rendered “Keroe.” The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide enough verse context to determine whether Keroe refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on reading the surrounding passage in Joshua.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “heading,” referring to something at the top or upper end of an object. It is used for a physical part or upper section rather than for a person’s leadership title. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 20 verses, including descriptions of furnishings and structures in Exodus and later passages in Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what object or section the surrounding text identifies.

This adjective means “spun,” describing material formed by twisting fibers or strands into thread. It is a rare word in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once, in Leviticus 14:6. Its basic sense identifies how the material was prepared rather than naming the material itself. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a description of something produced by spinning.

This Greek LXX adverb means “lightly” or “nimbly,” describing the manner in which someone or something moves or acts. It points to quickness or ease rather than heaviness or slowness. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 5:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic contribution is to show action carried out with lightness, agility, or swift movement.

This Greek LXX verb means to encircle or surround—to form a boundary around someone or something, or to move around it. It describes an action rather than a person, place, or object. The word occurs 73 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so its central sense is used across many kinds of passages. The exact force may refer to surrounding physically, circling an area, or enclosing something, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation.

This Greek LXX noun means “functionary” or “minister”: a person who performs an appointed service or carries out duties for others. It can describe an official servant in public or religious service, depending on the surrounding passage. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus. Its central idea is not merely serving casually, but fulfilling a recognized role or responsibility. The exact responsibility intended in any particular verse must be understood from that passage’s context.

Makrōn is a proper name, referring to a person named Makron. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles 17:17 and once in 2 Maccabees 10:12. Without the surrounding verse text, these references establish the name’s use but do not provide further detail about Makron’s identity or role.

“Drunkenness” means the condition of being intoxicated, especially through excessive drinking. It is a noun describing this state rather than the drink itself or the act of drinking. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs nine times, including passages in Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject. The same English rendering, “drunkenness,” confirms this central sense in the available translation support.

Melchiēl, also rendered Melkhil, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object, so its main function is personal identification. This name occurs three times in the Greek LXX, in Genesis 46:17, Numbers 26:29, and 1 Chronicles 7:31. The supplied lexical definition gives the name itself rather than an additional explanation of its meaning.

This Greek LXX noun means “change” or “changing”—a movement from one condition, situation, or state to another. It names the process or reality of alteration rather than describing a person or object itself. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures represented here, including passages in Esther, Isaiah, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being changed and the surrounding wording.

This adjective describes something marked by blood—“blood-stained” or “bloody.” It identifies a person, object, or situation by its visible connection with blood, while the surrounding passage determines the precise force intended. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its uses are recorded at 2 Maccabees 4:38 and 12:6, but the verse text is needed to explain what is being described in each place.

Nabat, also rendered Navat, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical usage. The name occurs 30 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing mainly in 1 and 2 Kings, with additional occurrences in 2 Chronicles and Sirach. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes the individual called Nabat within the biblical accounts. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role in each occurrence.

This verb means “nod off,” describing the act of becoming sleepy or slipping into sleep. It refers to a person’s loss of alertness rather than to an object or idea. In the Septuagint, it occurs 11 times: 10 times in the Old Testament and once in the deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any verse is understood from the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “lament” or “bewail”: it describes expressing deep sorrow or mourning. It presents grief as an active response, such as grieving openly over a painful loss or situation, rather than simply naming sadness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 38:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an expression of earnest sorrow.

This noun refers to a donkey-centaur, a mythic creature imagined as part donkey and part human. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in Isaiah, in descriptions of desolate or ruined places. The word identifies a creature associated with the imagery of abandoned wilderness, but the precise force of each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its meaning is therefore specific rather than a general word for an ordinary animal or person.

“Signet cord” refers to a cord associated with a signet, such as a seal or ring used for identification. The word is a noun, so it names this object rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs five times, with occurrences in Genesis, Proverbs, and Song of Songs. Its precise use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX particle means “then.” It marks what follows in sequence, linking one statement or action with what comes next. As a connecting word, its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic role is to signal progression or consequence in the flow of thought. It occurs 233 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, showing that it is a regularly used narrative and explanatory connector.

gl: rear guard; bring up the rear
d: rear guard; bring up the rear

e.t: This verb means to serve as the rear guard—to bring up the rear of a group or procession. It describes the action of staying behind the main body to guard or accompany those at the back. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears twice: once in Joshua and once in Sirach. The surrounding verse is needed to show exactly who is performing this role, but the central idea remains movement or protection at the rear.

This adjective means “totally abominable”: it describes something viewed as utterly detestable or disgusting. It is a strongly negative description, not a mild criticism or a neutral label. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, in 4 Maccabees 10:17. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its basic sense is clear: complete abhorrence or extreme repugnance.

The word means “disregard”: to refuse to give something the attention or obedience it calls for. As a verb, it describes setting aside a word, instruction, warning, or claim rather than responding to it. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs five times, in five verses across Esther and Isaiah. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being disregarded and the surrounding sentence.

This noun refers to “rage” or “provocation”—intense anger or conduct that stirs another person to anger. It can describe an angry outburst itself or an action that provokes such a response, so the central idea is heated offense and the reaction it creates. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, across Kings, Nehemiah, and Jeremiah. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation.

This noun means “any kind of dressed food”—food that has been prepared or made ready to eat. It names a category of prepared food rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times in five verses, with most occurrences in Ezekiel and one in Hosea. The surrounding verse determines what particular prepared food is intended, but the word itself points generally to food that has received preparation. Its meaning is therefore practical and concrete: a prepared food item or portion.

This verb means to control or to be superior to someone or something. It describes having the stronger position, authority, or effective power in a situation. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs five times, all in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on exercising control or on prevailing over another. Its basic idea is superiority expressed through mastery or dominance.

This word is the proper name “Petra.” It functions as a name rather than as a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 88 times, beginning in Exodus and continuing through Song of Songs. The name appears across many books, including Psalms, Isaiah, Judges, Job, and Jeremiah. Its exact reference in any passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “about.” It indicates an approximate place, point, or circumstance rather than identifying something with exact precision. As an adverb, it modifies the surrounding statement by adding this sense of general location or approximation. It appears 113 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a commonly used word for expressing “about” in different settings.

This verb means to “look ahead”—to direct one’s attention toward what lies in front. It describes an act of anticipating or viewing something ahead rather than simply observing what is immediately present. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in Psalm 36:13. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains the forward-looking action expressed by “look ahead.”

This verb means “live among,” describing the act of residing or dwelling in the midst of other people. It presents living among others as an action rather than naming a person, place, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 14:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on dwelling among a community or group.

This Greek LXX verb means “leave besides as a legacy.” It describes leaving something behind for others as a continuing legacy. Because it is a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Exodus 36:7. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains the act of leaving something behind as a legacy.

This Greek LXX verb means “go to” or “approach.” It describes movement toward a person or place, whether someone comes near, joins others, or proceeds toward a destination. The word occurs four times in the LXX corpus, including passages from 1 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains straightforward: someone moves nearer or goes toward something. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is simply on arrival, coming alongside others, or advancing toward a particular place.

Rabba, also given as Rhavva, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a specific name rather than a general description, action, or quality. This LXX word appears five times across four verses, including passages in Joshua, 1 Chronicles, and Amos. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide verse text or surrounding context, its precise reference in any particular passage must be understood from that passage itself.

“Tsebaoth” is a noun used as a distinctive designation in the Greek Old Testament. Its lexical meaning is given as “Tsebaoth,” so the word is normally preserved as a name or title rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive English term. It occurs 61 times in the LXX corpus, with most occurrences appearing in Isaiah. The word is found from Joshua through Jeremiah, showing continued use across several Old Testament books.

Salmaa is a proper name—the personal name of someone identified in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Salmaa” and does not function as a general description, action, or abstract idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 15:26. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further; its basic meaning is the name itself, Salmaa.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Sebēma” or “Sevima.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 31:32. The available information identifies its name-form and location, but does not establish whether the named entity is a person, place, or another specific designation. Its precise identification therefore depends on the surrounding verse text.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Sepphōr” or “Sepfor.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, title, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, from Numbers through Judges. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is identifying the person named, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular role or situation associated with that person.

In the Greek Old Testament, “stiff-necked” describes someone who is resistant and unwilling to bend or respond readily to direction. It is an adjective used of a person or people, portraying a settled posture rather than a physical neck condition. This word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, giving it a consistent sense of stubborn resistance. Its primary meaning is clearly “stiff-necked.”

Sor is a proper name used to identify a particular named entity, rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears ten times, with most occurrences in Ezekiel and one in Jeremiah. The available rendering preserves the name as “Sor,” so no broader descriptive meaning is established here. Its precise identity or significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “groan”: to express pain, distress, or deep inward burden with an audible sound. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is used across several settings while retaining this central sense. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Syllem, also rendered Sillim, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a specific named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name appears once in the Greek LXX, at Genesis 46:24. The available lexical information establishes its name form and function, while the surrounding verse would be needed to identify precisely whom or what the name designates there.

This verb means “wail”: to express grief or distress with a loud cry. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 13:8, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself plainly conveys vocal expression of intense sorrow or anguish.

This is a proper name rendered “Syriakē” or “Siriaki.” It identifies something by that name rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Job 42:17 and once in 2 Maccabees 15:36. Without the verse text and surrounding context, the name alone does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, language, or people. Its precise reference must therefore be determined from each passage.

The word therefore describes land as an allotted domain, not an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 11 times. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This word means “four,” the number that identifies a quantity of four persons, objects, or units. It can function as a number describing something counted, and in some sentences it may stand in for the group or things being counted. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 224 times, showing regular use wherever a group or measurement of four is mentioned. Its exact reference depends on the noun or objects described in the surrounding verse.

This adjective means “for the bow,” describing something connected with or intended for a bow. It is a specific descriptive term rather than a broad word for weapons or warfare. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Judges 5:28. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence must be understood from its context, but its basic meaning remains something related to a bow.

This word means “on the contrary.” It marks a contrast, signaling that what follows—or what is being described—stands against an earlier statement or expectation. As an adjective, it identifies something as opposite or contrary rather than agreeing with what came before. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:22. The exact force of the contrast in that verse depends on its surrounding wording, but the word itself plainly points to opposition or a reversal of the preceding idea.

This Greek LXX noun refers to the essential nature or underlying structure of something—the reality that supports or gives it substance. Its basic sense can describe what stands beneath or constitutes a thing, rather than merely its outward appearance. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. Its stated meanings are “essence” and “substructure.”

This adverb means “mixedly” or “in utter confusion.” It describes an action or situation as disorderly, jumbled, or lacking clear arrangement. Rather than naming a person or object, it tells how something happens or appears. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:41. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is clear: things are mixed together in a confused and disorganized way.

This Greek LXX noun refers to “stock of papyrus; paper,” a writing material made from papyrus. It names the material itself rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 4:20. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, its precise use in that passage cannot be described further, but its ordinary meaning is the papyrus material or paper being referred to.

This adjective describes something as made of grass, resembling grass, or having the character of grass. Its central idea is a comparison with grass rather than a person, action, or abstract quality. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 5:27; the reference identifies its sole occurrence, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain what it describes there. The basic meaning remains “of grass; grass-like.”

This noun means a drop—a small amount of liquid falling or resting in one place. It is used in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) for something noticed as drops, whether falling from above or present upon a surface. The word occurs twice in this corpus, once in Job and once in Song of Songs. Its basic sense remains simple and physical: a single drop or drops of liquid, with the surrounding verse supplying the precise setting.

Ōn, or On, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as a name, while the surrounding passage determines the specific referent. This name occurs 426 times across 410 verses in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its lexical meaning is simply “Ōn; On.”
